title: Al-Baqarah: Covenant, Law, the Throne Verse and "No Compulsion"
bigQuestion: How does the longest surah hold story, law, prayer and argument together, and why has one of its verses been debated for 1,400 years?

story.title: One Verse, Fourteen Centuries
story.kicker: The longest chapter in the book contains a short line that readers have argued over since the seventh century.
paragraphs: A student in a Chicago high school opens a copy of Pickthall's translation for a research paper. She turns past the seven short lines of Al-Fatiha and lands in Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, The Cow. It runs for 286 verses, more than forty pages in most printings. Her teacher has told her the surah is a kind of map of the whole Qur'an. Almost every theme in the book appears here: creation, prophets, prayer, fasting, money, marriage, war, and the last day.

She reads the opening. The surah begins with three Arabic letters, Alif, Lam, Mim, whose meaning Muslim scholars say only God knows for certain. Then comes a sentence that sets the tone: this is the Book in which there is no doubt, a guidance for those who guard themselves against wrong. From the first line, the surah speaks as a text that expects to be obeyed, not just admired.

Halfway down verse 256 she stops. In Pickthall's English it reads: There is no compulsion in religion. She has heard the phrase before, on the news and in a documentary. Now she sees where it sits: right after the Throne Verse, the most-recited single verse in the Muslim world, and in the middle of a chapter full of rules for a new community in Medina.

Her research turns up a surprise. The line has been read many ways. Classical commentators, such as al-Tabari in the tenth century, collected stories about the moment it was revealed. A few early scholars thought later verses limited it. Most, then and now, read it as a standing principle: faith cannot be forced. Modern Muslim writers quote it in debates about religious freedom. The student realizes her paper is not about one verse. It is about how a community reads its own book, and keeps reading it, for fourteen hundred years.
story.think: Why might a short, clear-sounding verse still be read in different ways by serious readers across many centuries?

sections.title: The Shape of the Longest Surah

lessons.title: A Medinan Surah
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Baqarah is the longest surah, revealed over several years in Medina, and its voice is the voice of a community learning to live by law.
reading: Surah 2 is called *Al-Baqarah*, The Cow. The name comes from a story inside it (2:67–73), in which the Children of Israel are told to sacrifice a cow and ask question after question about which cow. Surahs are usually named after a striking word or story in them, not after their main subject. With 286 ayahs, Al-Baqarah is the longest surah in the Qur'an. In most printed copies it fills the first two and a half of the thirty parts, or *juz'*, that Muslims use to read the book across a month.

Muslim tradition places the surah in the *Medinan* period. In 622, according to the sira, the traditional biography, Muhammad and his followers left Mecca for the town of Yathrib, later called Medina. Scholars count the surahs revealed before that move as Meccan and those after it as Medinan. Al-Baqarah is usually described as one of the earliest Medinan surahs, though tradition says its verses came over several years, and some readers note that a few of its verses may be among the last revealed.

The difference in voice is easy to hear. Meccan surahs are often short, urgent and poetic. They warn, call to one God, and describe the last day. Medinan surahs are longer and address a community that now had land, a mosque, neighbors and enemies. Al-Baqarah opens with the phrase O ye who believe many times, and it gives rules: how to fast, how to write a contract, how to treat a divorced wife, when fighting is allowed. Historians note that this fits what the sira describes: a new community working out how to live together.

words.d: Surah 2, The Cow; the longest surah, with 286 ayahs
a surah that Muslim tradition dates after the move to Medina in 622
one of thirty roughly equal parts of the Qur'an used for reading it over a month

look.title: How Long Is Al-Baqarah?
look.cite: Verse counts as printed in the standard Cairo edition (1924) and in Pickthall (1930)
look.prompt: Al-Baqarah has more ayahs than the next two longest surahs together. What does its size suggest about its role in the book?

check.q: Why is Surah 2 called The Cow?
choices: Because a story inside it tells of the Israelites and a cow
Because cows were sacred in Medina
Because its first word is cow
Because it lists the animals Muslims may eat
check.why: Surahs take their names from a striking word or story; here it is the cow story in 2:67–73.

check.q: What does Medinan mean when applied to a surah?
choices: Written by the people of Medina
Revealed, by tradition, after the move to Medina in 622
check.why: Muslim scholars sort surahs by whether tradition dates them before or after the hijra of 622.

check.q: Which feature is typical of Medinan surahs like Al-Baqarah?
choices: Very short verses about the last day
Being placed at the end of the book
check.why: Medinan surahs address a community with land and neighbors, so they contain law on fasting, contracts and family.

lessons.title: The Opening Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Baqarah opens with mysterious letters, a claim about the book itself, and a portrait of three kinds of listener.
reading: Al-Baqarah begins with three Arabic letters, Alif, Lam, Mim. Twenty-nine surahs open with letters like these, called the *disconnected letters*. Muslim commentators have offered many readings: that they are abbreviations, that they point to the Arabic alphabet the Qur'an is built from, or that their meaning is known only to God. Most classical commentators, including al-Tabari, list several views and do not pick one. Modern scholars have added theories, but no reading has won general agreement.

The second ayah makes a claim about the book. In Pickthall's translation: This is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt, a guidance unto those who ward off (evil). The Arabic word Pickthall renders as ward off evil is *taqwa*, often translated as God-consciousness or mindfulness. The verse does not argue that the book is true; it states it and moves on. Readers who study rhetoric note that this is a common Qur'anic move: the text speaks with authority and expects assent.

Verses 3 through 20 then describe three groups. First come those who believe, pray and give: the text says guidance is for them. Then come those who reject the message, of whom the surah says warning will not help. Then, at greater length, come people who say they believe but do not: the *hypocrites*, in Arabic munafiqun. The surah gives them two parables, a man who lights a fire and loses its light, and travelers caught in a storm. Commentators read these verses as a portrait of Medina's mixed population, where the new community lived beside those who had joined it half-heartedly.

words.d: single Arabic letters that open 29 surahs; their meaning is debated
mindfulness of God; guarding oneself against wrong
in the Qur'an, people who claim faith they do not hold (Arabic munafiqun)

look.title: The Book Speaks of Itself
look.text: This is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt, a guidance unto those who ward off (evil).
look.cite: Qur'an 2:2, Al-Baqarah, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: The verse says who the guidance is for. Who is named, and who is left out? How does this shape the way the rest of the surah speaks?

check.q: What do most classical commentators say about the letters Alif, Lam, Mim?
choices: They are the name of the scribe
They spell the word for cow
They mark the surah as Meccan
Several readings exist and their meaning is not settled
check.why: Al-Tabari and others list many views on the disconnected letters and do not settle on one.

check.q: In 2:2, for whom does the text say the book is a guidance?
choices: For those who ward off evil, people of taqwa
For every person who reads it
check.why: Pickthall renders 2:2 as guidance unto those who ward off (evil), the Arabic taqwa.

check.q: Who are the hypocrites in the opening of Al-Baqarah?
choices: People who claim faith but do not hold it
check.why: The munafiqun are described as saying they believe while not believing; commentators tie this to Medina's mixed population.

lessons.title: Reading in Sequence
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Baqarah moves from creation and prophets to law and prayer; reading verses in order shows how each section prepares the next.
reading: Many people meet Qur'an verses one at a time, on a poster, in a speech or on a screen. Reading a surah in *sequence* is different. Scholars who study the structure of the Qur'an, from medieval commentators to modern readers, have argued that Al-Baqarah has a plan. The details differ, but a common outline runs like this: an opening on the book and its listeners (1–39), the Children of Israel and their covenant (40–123), Ibrahim (Abraham) and the Ka'bah (124–152), law for the new community (153–283), and a closing statement of faith and prayer (284–286).

Read this way, the middle of the surah makes sense. Before the text tells the believers how to pray, fast and fight, it tells them how an earlier people received a law and what happened when they kept or broke it. Then it tells how Ibrahim, whom the Qur'an calls neither Jew nor Christian but one who submitted to God, built the Ka'bah in Mecca. Only after that does the surah announce a new direction for prayer and a new set of rules. The story explains the law.

Some modern scholars, such as those who study *ring composition*, argue that the surah's parts mirror each other, with the change of qibla near the center. Others are cautious and say readers should not force a pattern onto a text gathered from several years of revelation. Both groups agree on one thing: to understand a verse of Al-Baqarah, read the verses around it. This chapter follows that rule.

words.d: the order in which verses appear; reading in sequence means following that order
a structure in which parts of a text mirror each other around a center
the cube-shaped shrine in Mecca that the Qur'an says Ibrahim and Isma'il built

look.title: A Map of Al-Baqarah
look.text: One common outline of Surah 2: (1) verses 1–39, the book, its listeners, and the story of Adam; (2) verses 40–123, the Children of Israel and their covenant; (3) verses 124–152, Ibrahim, the Ka'bah and the new qibla; (4) verses 153–283, law for the community: fasting, pilgrimage, marriage, debt, fighting; (5) verses 284–286, a closing statement of faith and a prayer.
look.prompt: Why might the surah tell the story of an earlier covenant before giving its own community new laws? What is a reader supposed to carry from part 2 into part 4?

check.q: In a common outline of Al-Baqarah, what comes right before the section of laws?
check.why: Verses 124–152 on Ibrahim and the Ka'bah lead into the qibla change and then the laws that begin around verse 153.

check.q: What do scholars who see ring composition in Al-Baqarah claim?
choices: The surah repeats one verse in a loop
It has no plan at all
It was written in a circle on early manuscripts
Its parts mirror each other around a center
check.why: Ring composition is the idea that sections mirror each other around a central point, here near the qibla verses.

check.q: What rule for reading do both careful and cautious scholars share?
choices: Read a verse with the verses around it
check.why: Whatever they think of larger patterns, scholars agree that context within the surah matters.

lessons.title: Adam and the Angels
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Baqarah tells the story of Adam as the first human, taught the names of things and placed on earth as God's viceroy.
reading: In 2:30–39 the surah tells of Adam. In Pickthall's translation, God says to the angels: Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth. The Arabic word is *khalifah*, one who stands in for another, later used for the rulers of the Muslim community. The angels ask why God would place one who will do harm and shed blood, while they praise God. God answers that He knows what they do not.

Then God teaches Adam the names of all things and asks the angels to name them. They cannot; Adam can. The angels are told to bow to Adam, and all do except *Iblis*, who refuses. The Qur'an elsewhere says Iblis was of the jinn and was too proud to bow to a being made of clay. Adam and his wife live in the Garden, are told not to approach one tree, are misled by Satan, and are sent down to earth. Then, the surah says, Adam received words from his Lord and God relented toward him.

Readers of the Bible will notice both likeness and difference. Genesis 2–3 also has a garden, a forbidden tree and an expulsion. But the Qur'an's telling has no serpent, no talking of the tree of knowledge, and it names no woman as the first to eat. Most Muslim commentators, from al-Tabari on, stress that Adam repented and was forgiven, and that the Qur'an teaches no inherited guilt. Christian readers of Genesis, by contrast, have often read the story as the beginning of a fallen condition. Comparing the two texts shows how each tradition builds a different teaching from a shared story.

words.d: a deputy or one who stands in for another; Pickthall's viceroy; later the title of Muslim rulers
the being who refused to bow to Adam; identified with Satan (Shaytan)
in the Qur'an, unseen beings made of fire, able to choose good or evil

look.title: A Viceroy in the Earth
look.text: And when thy Lord said unto the angels: Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth, they said: Wilt thou place therein one who will do harm therein and will shed blood, while we, we hymn Thy praise and sanctify Thee? He said: Surely I know that which ye know not.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:30, Al-Baqarah, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: The angels object and God does not explain. What does the next verse, in which Adam names things, suggest is the answer?

check.q: What does the Arabic word khalifah, Pickthall's viceroy, mean?
choices: One who stands in for another
check.why: Khalifah means a deputy or successor; the same word later named the rulers of the Muslim community.

check.q: Which element is in Genesis 2–3 but not in Al-Baqarah's Adam story?
check.why: The Qur'an's telling has Satan misleading the pair but no serpent; garden, tree and expulsion appear in both.

check.q: How do most Muslim commentators read the end of the Adam story?
choices: Adam's guilt passed to all his children
check.why: 2:37 says Adam received words and God relented toward him; commentators stress forgiveness and no inherited guilt.

lessons.title: The Children of Israel
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Baqarah retells Israel's covenant at length, praising its gifts and criticizing its breaking, as a lesson aimed at the new community.
reading: From verse 40 to about verse 123, the surah addresses the *Children of Israel*, Banu Isra'il. The passage opens with a reminder of favor: remember My favor that I bestowed on you, and keep your covenant with Me. It then retells episodes known from the Hebrew Bible: rescue from Pharaoh, the parting of the sea, manna and quails, water from the rock, the golden calf, and Musa (Moses) receiving the Book. The surah's own name comes from this stretch, in the story of the cow the people were told to sacrifice.

The tone is mixed. The text calls Israel a people God preferred above all creatures (2:47) and, in the same breath, lists moments when the people broke their *covenant*, their binding agreement with God. It says some of them changed the words of scripture, killed prophets, or claimed the fire would touch them only a few days. Historians note that the surah is speaking, according to the sira, at a time when the Muslim community in Medina lived beside Jewish tribes who had not accepted Muhammad's claim. The argument is with those neighbors.

How should a reader handle this? Muslim commentators have long said the passage warns Muslims as much as anyone: a people given a book can lose its way. Modern scholars, Muslim and non-Muslim, stress that the verses address particular groups in a particular dispute, not every Jew in every time, and they point to 2:62, which says that Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe in God and the last day and do right will have their reward. Reading the whole stretch, rather than a single verse, is the only fair way to hear it.

words.d: Banu Isra'il; the descendants of Ya'qub (Jacob), addressed at length in Al-Baqarah
a binding agreement; in the Qur'an, the bond between God and a people who receive a book
the traditional biography of Muhammad, compiled from the eighth century on

look.title: Two Verses, One Passage
look.text: Verse 2:47 tells the Children of Israel to remember that God favored them above all creatures. Verse 2:83 recalls their covenant to worship God alone, do good to parents, orphans and the needy, speak kindly, pray and give; then it says that most of them turned away. Verse 2:62 says that those who believe, and Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe in God and the last day and do right, have their reward with their Lord.
look.prompt: Put the three verses together. What is the passage praising, what is it criticizing, and how do commentators use 2:62 when explaining the harder verses?

check.q: What does the surah remind the Children of Israel of first, in 2:40?
check.why: 2:40 opens the address: remember My favor and fulfill your covenant with Me.

check.q: According to the sira, who is the surah arguing with in this stretch?
choices: Jewish tribes living beside the Muslims in Medina
check.why: Tradition places these verses in Medina, where Jewish tribes had not accepted Muhammad's claim to prophethood.

check.q: Which verse do modern scholars cite to show the passage is not a blanket judgment on Jews?
check.why: 2:62 says Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe in God and the last day and do right have their reward.

lessons.title: Ibrahim and the New Direction
lessons.mainIdea: The surah presents Ibrahim as builder of the Ka'bah, then announces the turn from Jerusalem to Mecca as the direction of prayer.
reading: Verses 124–141 tell of *Ibrahim* (Abraham). He is tested and made a leader for people. With his son Isma'il (Ishmael) he raises the foundations of the House, the Ka'bah in Mecca, and prays that a messenger will rise from his descendants. The surah then says Ibrahim was not a Jew or a Christian but a *hanif*, one who turned from idols to God alone, and that his religion is the religion the Qur'an calls people to. Muslims call the faith of Ibrahim the root of their own.

Then comes one of the few events in the surah that historians can date fairly well. According to the sira, for about sixteen or seventeen months after the move to Medina, Muslims prayed facing Jerusalem, the direction Jews prayed. In about 624, verses 142–150 announced a new *qibla*, the direction of prayer: the Sacred Mosque in Mecca. In Pickthall's rendering God says He has seen the Prophet turning his face to the sky and will now turn him toward a qibla that pleases him.

Commentators read the change several ways. Some say it answered the Prophet's own wish to face the House of his ancestor Ibrahim. Some see it as a mark of a community now distinct from its Jewish neighbors, who, the surah notes, would argue about it. The text itself gives a reason in 2:143: the earlier qibla was set to show who would follow the Messenger. Verse 177 adds that righteousness is not in facing east or west, but in faith, giving, prayer and keeping one's word. The direction matters; the surah also says it is not the point.

words.d: Abraham; in the Qur'an, a hanif who with Isma'il built the Ka'bah
one who turned from idols to the one God before Judaism or Christianity
the direction Muslims face in prayer; changed from Jerusalem to Mecca in about 624

look.title: Not East or West
look.text: Paraphrase of 2:177: It is not righteousness to turn your faces east or west. Righteous is the one who believes in God, the last day, the angels, the Book and the prophets; who gives wealth, for love of God, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler and those who ask, and to free captives; who keeps up prayer, gives the alms, keeps promises, and is patient in hardship and in war.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:177, Al-Baqarah, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: This verse comes soon after the qibla change. Why place a list of what righteousness really is right after a rule about which way to face?

check.q: What does the Qur'an mean by calling Ibrahim a hanif?
choices: One who turned from idols to God alone
check.why: 2:135 says Ibrahim was a hanif, not a Jew or Christian: one devoted to the one God.

check.q: Before about 624, which direction did Muslims in Medina face in prayer, according to the sira?
check.why: Tradition says Muslims faced Jerusalem for about sixteen months before verses 142–150 named Mecca.

check.q: What does 2:177 say about facing east or west?
choices: It is the whole of righteousness
It is not what righteousness consists of
It must be done at dawn
check.why: 2:177 says righteousness is not in the direction faced but in faith, giving, prayer and keeping one's word.

lessons.title: Fasting and Pilgrimage
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Baqarah sets out fasting in Ramadan and the rules of pilgrimage, presenting both as practices earlier peoples also knew.
reading: Verses 183–187 set out fasting. In Pickthall's translation: O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil). The verse ties the practice to earlier communities, which commentators take to include Jews and Christians. Verse 185 names the month: *Ramadan*, in which the Qur'an was sent down. Those who are sick or traveling may make up the days later. Verse 187 sets the hours, from the first light of dawn until night, and permits eating and marital relations at night.

Muslims read these verses every year. The fast, *sawm*, is one of the five practices Sunni tradition calls the pillars of Islam. In Chicago, as in every city with Muslim residents, mosques hold evening meals in Ramadan and the schedule of the fast shifts with the seasons, since the Islamic calendar is lunar and moves about eleven days earlier each solar year. Students who fast during the school day are a familiar sight in Illinois public schools.

Verses 196–203 turn to *hajj*, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and to umrah, the lesser visit. The surah gives practical rules: complete the rites, offer what animal you can, do not shave the head until the offering reaches its place, and if you cannot go, fast or feed the poor instead. It also warns against quarreling on the road and tells pilgrims to remember God at the places the rites move through. Historians note that pilgrimage to Mecca existed before Islam; the Qur'an, they say, kept the journey and refocused it on the one God and on Ibrahim.

words.d: the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, in which Muslims fast from dawn to night
fasting; abstaining from food, drink and marital relations in daylight
the pilgrimage to Mecca, required once in a lifetime of Muslims who are able

look.title: As It Was Prescribed Before
look.text: O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil).
look.cite: Qur'an 2:183, Al-Baqarah, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: The verse says fasting was prescribed for earlier peoples. Why might a new community's law begin by pointing to older ones?

check.q: What reason does 2:183 give for fasting?
choices: To ward off evil, that is, to gain taqwa
check.why: Pickthall's that ye may ward off (evil) renders the Arabic word for taqwa, mindfulness of God.

check.q: Why does the date of Ramadan move each year on the school calendar?
choices: Each mosque chooses its own month
check.why: 2:185 names Ramadan, a month of a lunar calendar that shifts about eleven days earlier each solar year.

check.q: What do historians say about pilgrimage to Mecca before Islam?
choices: It already existed and the Qur'an refocused it
It was banned by the Romans
check.why: Historians note pre-Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca; the Qur'an ties the rites to Ibrahim and the one God.

lessons.title: Family and Debt
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Baqarah gives detailed rules on marriage, divorce and lending, including the longest verse in the Qur'an, on writing down a debt.
reading: Verses 221–242 deal with marriage and divorce. The surah sets a waiting period, *iddah*, of three monthly cycles after a divorce, during which a wife stays in the home and may be taken back. It limits a husband to two revocable divorces, then a final one. It says a husband must not hold a wife to harm her, tells both sides to part with kindness, and provides for a divorced woman and for nursing mothers. Commentators note that in the Arabia the sira describes, these rules set limits where there had been few. Modern readers, including Muslim women scholars, debate how the rules apply today; the law schools of Islam have differed on details for centuries.

Verse 275 forbids *riba*, usually translated usury or interest, and contrasts it with trade, which is allowed. Verses 276–281 warn those who take riba and tell lenders to give a struggling debtor time, or to forgive the debt as charity. How riba applies to modern banking is a live debate: some Muslim scholars hold that all bank interest is riba, others that only exploitative rates are, and an industry of Islamic finance has grown up around the question.

Verse 282 is the longest single ayah in the Qur'an. It tells believers who contract a debt for a fixed term to write it down, to have a scribe write fairly, to have the debtor dictate, and to call two witnesses. If two men are not available, it says, then one man and two women, so that if one forgets the other may remind her. This clause has been read in many ways: classical jurists built rules of testimony on it, while many modern scholars argue it addresses the commercial experience of women in seventh-century Arabia, not their capacity. The verse ends by saying that writing is fairer and reduces doubt.

words.d: the waiting period after divorce or widowhood before a woman may remarry
usury or interest on loans, forbidden in 2:275; its scope is debated
a person who observes an agreement and can testify to it; 2:282 calls for two

look.title: Two Readings of One Clause
look.text: 2:282 says that a written debt should have two witnesses, and if two men are not at hand, one man and two women, so that if one errs the other may remind her. Reading A, held by many classical jurists: this sets a general rule for testimony in financial cases. Reading B, held by many modern scholars: the clause reflects the trading experience of women in seventh-century Arabia and gives a practical safeguard, not a statement about capacity.
look.prompt: What does each reading assume about how a verse's context should shape its application? Which parts of the verse could support each?

check.q: What is riba, forbidden in 2:275?
choices: Usury or interest on a loan
check.why: 2:275 contrasts riba, usually translated usury or interest, with trade, which the verse allows.

check.q: What is special about 2:282?
choices: It is the shortest verse in the Qur'an
It is the longest verse in the Qur'an
It names the month of Ramadan
check.why: Verse 282, on writing down a debt, is the longest single ayah in the book.

check.q: What does the surah tell a lender to do for a debtor in hardship?
choices: Report the debtor to the judge
Give time or forgive the debt as charity
check.why: 2:280 says to grant time to a debtor in difficulty and adds that forgiving the debt is better.

lessons.title: When Fighting Is Allowed
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Baqarah's verses on fighting are tied to the war with Mecca and set limits; readers argue about how far those limits reach.
reading: Verses 190–194 speak of fighting. In Pickthall's rendering, believers are told to fight in the way of God those who fight them, but not to begin hostilities, for God does not love aggressors. The verses allow fighting near the Sacred Mosque only if the other side fights there first, tell believers to stop if the other side stops, and say that fighting should continue until there is no more *fitnah*, persecution, and religion is for God. Verse 216 says fighting is ordained though it is hateful to the believers.

The sira places these verses after the Muslims' move to Medina, when they were at war with the Meccan clans who had driven them out. The Battle of Badr, in about 624, is the first major clash tradition records. Verse 217 addresses an incident in the sacred months and 2:244–246 recall how the Israelites asked for a king to fight for them. Historians note that the verses read as responses to a conflict already underway, with the Sacred Mosque still in Meccan hands.

Readers differ over scope. Most classical jurists read the limits, do not begin hostilities and stop when they stop, as binding and built laws of war on them: no killing of noncombatants, no breaking of treaties. A minority of medieval scholars held that later verses in Surah 9 widened permission; most mainstream scholars, past and present, deny this and say the Surah 9 verses also address specific enemies. Modern Muslim scholars almost without exception read 2:190 as the governing verse: fighting is defensive and bounded. This course reports the readings; the debate belongs to the tradition.

words.d: persecution, trial or strife; in 2:193, the persecution that fighting is meant to end
one who begins hostilities; 2:190 says God does not love aggressors
the first major battle between the Muslims of Medina and the Meccans, c. 624

look.title: Reading 2:190 in Context
look.text: Paraphrase of 2:190–193: Fight in God's way those who fight you, but do not begin hostilities; God does not love aggressors. Do not fight at the Sacred Mosque unless they fight you there. If they stop, God is forgiving and merciful. Fight until persecution ends and religion is for God; but if they stop, let there be no hostility except against wrongdoers. Two readers: a classical jurist says the phrase until persecution ends sets the goal; a modern scholar says the repeated if they stop sets the limit.
look.prompt: Which clauses in the passage support each reader? What would change if you read verse 190 alone, without 191–193?

check.q: What limit does 2:190 place on fighting?
choices: Do not begin hostilities; fight those who fight you
Fight only in the sacred months
check.why: 2:190 tells believers to fight those who fight them and not to be aggressors.

check.q: What situation does the sira attach to these verses?
choices: The war between Medina and the Meccan clans
A dispute with the Christians of Najran
check.why: Tradition places 2:190–194 in the years of conflict with Mecca, around the Battle of Badr in about 624.

check.q: How do most mainstream scholars, past and present, read 2:190?
choices: As applying only to the Israelites
As the governing rule: fighting is defensive and bounded
check.why: Most jurists and modern scholars treat the limits in 2:190 as binding, against a minority who thought Surah 9 widened them.

sections.title: Two Famous Verses and a Prayer

lessons.title: The Throne Verse
lessons.mainIdea: Ayat al-Kursi, 2:255, is the most recited single verse in the Muslim world; it describes God's knowledge, power and care in one sentence.
reading: Verse 255 is called *Ayat al-Kursi*, the Throne Verse, from the word kursi, throne or footstool, near its end. Muslims recite it after daily prayers, before sleep, and over the sick; many hadith reports, paraphrased, call it the greatest verse in the Qur'an. It hangs on the walls of homes and shops from Chicago to Jakarta, often in calligraphy. It is one of the first long verses Muslim children memorize.

The verse begins with the core of Muslim belief, *tawhid*, the oneness of God: Allah, there is no God save Him. It goes on to describe God as living and self-sustaining, never overtaken by slumber or sleep, owner of all in the heavens and the earth. No one intercedes with Him except by His leave. He knows what lies before and behind His creatures, while they grasp only what He wills of His knowledge. His throne, or kursi, extends over the heavens and the earth, and preserving them does not tire Him. He is the Sublime, the Tremendous.

Commentators have paused on the word kursi. Some early readers took it as a literal footstool before God's greater throne, the arsh; others, including many later theologians, read it as a figure for God's knowledge or dominion. Sufi writers have read the verse as a meditation on God's presence. The verse's place is also noticed: it sits just before no compulsion in religion. Some readers see a pairing, a statement of who God is followed by a statement that faith in Him cannot be forced.

words.d: the Throne Verse, 2:255, the most recited single verse in Muslim practice
the oneness of God, the central teaching of Islam
throne or footstool; read literally by some commentators and as a figure by others

look.title: The Throne Verse Opens
look.text: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Unto Him belongeth whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is in the earth. Who is he that intercedeth with Him save by His leave? He knoweth that which is in front of them and that which is behind them, while they encompass nothing of His knowledge save what He will.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:255 (first part), Al-Baqarah, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: List the qualities of God the verse names, in order. Which ones concern power and which concern knowledge? Why might a verse like this be chosen for daily recitation?

check.q: Why is 2:255 called the Throne Verse?
choices: It describes a king's throne in Medina
It names the angel who holds the throne
It was revealed on a throne
It contains the word kursi, throne or footstool
check.why: The name Ayat al-Kursi comes from the word kursi near the end of the verse.

check.q: Which teaching does the Throne Verse open with?
check.why: The verse begins Allah! There is no God save Him, the statement of tawhid.

check.q: How have commentators differed on the word kursi?
choices: All agree it means a chair in the Ka'bah
Some read it as a literal footstool, others as a figure for knowledge or rule
It is read as the name of a city
It is read as the name of a scribe
check.why: Early readers took kursi literally; many later theologians and Sufis read it as a figure.

lessons.title: No Compulsion in Religion
lessons.mainIdea: Verse 2:256 says there is no compulsion in religion; commentators have read it as a report of an occasion, a limited rule, or a lasting principle.
reading: Verse 256, in Pickthall's translation, begins: There is no compulsion in religion. The right direction is henceforth distinct from error. It goes on to say that whoever rejects false gods and believes in God has grasped a firm handhold that will not break. The Arabic word for compulsion is *ikrah*, forcing. The verse follows the Throne Verse and comes near the end of the surah's long section of laws.

Classical commentators asked what occasion produced it. Al-Tabari, writing in about 900, collected several reports. In one, women of the Ansar, the Medinan helpers, had vowed before Islam to raise a child among the Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir if the child lived; when that tribe was expelled, some fathers wanted to force those children to become Muslim, and the verse forbade it. Another report has a man wanting to compel his two sons who had become Christian. Al-Tabari chose the reading that the verse forbids forcing the People of the Book and others who pay the poll tax. A few early scholars held that the verse was *abrogated*, that is, set aside, by later verses commanding fighting. Most rejected that view; Ibn Kathir, in the fourteenth century, wrote that no one is to be forced into Islam because its proofs are clear.

Modern readers have made the verse central. Muslim scholars in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries cite it in arguments for religious freedom and against forced conversion, and many national constitutions in Muslim-majority countries echo it. Critics note that some classical jurists still punished leaving Islam, and ask how that squares with the verse; Muslim scholars answer in different ways, some defending the old rule, many arguing that it rested on treason in wartime, not on belief. The verse itself is short. What readers bring to it, and which other verses they read it beside, decides what they hear.

words.d: compulsion or forcing; the word in 2:256 that the verse says has no place in religion
set aside by a later verse; a classical theory (naskh) that some verses replace earlier ones
a report, collected by commentators, of the event that a verse answered

look.title: A Firm Handhold
look.text: There is no compulsion in religion. The right direction is henceforth distinct from error. And he who rejecteth false deities and believeth in Allah hath grasped a firm handhold which will never break. Allah is Hearer, Knower.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:256, Al-Baqarah, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: The verse gives a reason right after its rule: the right direction is now distinct from error. How does that reason support the rule, in the eyes of a commentator like Ibn Kathir?

check.q: What did al-Tabari collect to explain 2:256?
choices: A list of the surah's names
Reports of the occasion that produced the verse
check.why: Commentators like al-Tabari gathered occasion-of-revelation reports, such as the story of the Ansar children raised among Banu Nadir.

check.q: What does it mean to say a verse is abrogated?
choices: It was lost from the manuscripts
It is set aside by a later verse
check.why: Abrogation, naskh, is the classical theory that a later verse can replace an earlier ruling; most scholars did not apply it to 2:256.

check.q: How do most Muslim scholars, from Ibn Kathir to today, read 2:256?
choices: As a rule against forcing anyone into Islam
check.why: Ibn Kathir wrote that no one is to be forced into Islam, and modern scholars cite the verse for religious freedom.

lessons.title: The Closing Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Baqarah ends with a statement of what the believers accept and a prayer that asks not to be burdened beyond one's strength.
reading: The surah closes in verses 284–286. Verse 285 states what the Messenger and the believers accept: God, His angels, His books and His messengers, making no distinction between any of His messengers. Muslim readers point out that this line names the same list found in the earliest creeds of Islam. Verse 286 then turns into a *prayer*, spoken in the voice of the community: Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err; do not lay on us a burden like the one laid on those before us; do not load us with more than we can bear; pardon us, forgive us, have mercy on us; You are our Protector, so help us against the people who reject faith.

The prayer begins with a principle many Muslims quote: God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Jurists have built on it when discussing hardship, illness and travel, the same cases the fasting verses allowed for. Commentators also notice the phrase about a burden laid on those before us. Most read it as a reference back to the Children of Israel, addressed earlier in the surah, and to the heavier law the Qur'an says they carried. The end of the surah answers its middle.

Hadith reports, paraphrased, say the Prophet called the last two verses of Al-Baqarah a special gift and recommended reciting them at night. Many Muslims still do. For a student reading in sequence, the ending does something else. A surah that opened with three letters and a claim about the book ends with a community speaking in the first person to God. The text has moved from address to response.

words.d: here, a plea to God spoken in the voice of the community, as in 2:286
in Islam, those sent by God with a message; 2:285 says believers make no distinction among them
what a person is able to bear; 2:286 says God burdens no soul beyond it

look.title: No Burden Beyond Strength
look.text: Paraphrase of 2:286: God does not task a soul beyond what it can bear. Each soul has what it has earned, for it and against it. Our Lord, do not hold us to account if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord, do not lay on us a burden like the one You laid on those before us. Our Lord, do not load us with what we have no strength for. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector; help us against the people who reject faith.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:286, Al-Baqarah, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Which earlier parts of the surah does this prayer look back to? Find at least two connections.

check.q: What does 2:285 say the believers do about God's messengers?
check.why: 2:285 lists faith in God, angels, books and messengers, and says believers do not distinguish between His messengers.

check.q: Which principle opens the prayer in 2:286?
choices: God burdens no soul beyond its capacity
check.why: The verse begins by saying God does not task a soul beyond what it can bear.

check.q: Whom do most commentators think the burden laid on those before us refers to?
choices: The Children of Israel addressed earlier in the surah
check.why: Commentators read the phrase as looking back to the Children of Israel and the heavier law the Qur'an says they carried.

review.q: Which statement about Al-Baqarah is correct?
choices: It is the longest surah, dated by tradition to Medina
It is the shortest Meccan surah
It has no laws in it
It is named for the Throne Verse
review.why: Al-Baqarah has 286 ayahs and is placed in the Medinan period by Muslim tradition.

review.q: What did the Qur'an, in 2:30–34, say Adam could do that the angels could not?
choices: Name the things God had taught him
review.why: God taught Adam the names of all things; the angels could not name them, and were told to bow to him.

review.q: The change of qibla in about 624 turned prayer from which city to which?
review.why: Verses 142–150 announce the turn from Jerusalem, faced for about sixteen months, to the Sacred Mosque in Mecca.

review.q: Which practice does 2:183 say was also prescribed for earlier peoples?
review.why: 2:183: Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you.

review.q: What is the longest single verse in the Qur'an about?
choices: Writing down a debt with witnesses
review.why: 2:282, the longest ayah, tells believers to record a debt in writing with a scribe and witnesses.

review.q: What is the Arabic name of 2:255?
review.why: 2:255 is Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse, named for the word kursi.

review.q: A student says 2:256 was accepted by every classical scholar as a lasting rule with no debate. What is wrong with that claim?
choices: Nothing; there was never any debate
The verse is not in Al-Baqarah
A few early scholars argued it was abrogated, though most rejected that view
review.why: Most commentators read 2:256 as standing, but a minority held it was set aside by later fighting verses.

choices: With the story of the cow
With a prayer in the community's voice asking not to be burdened beyond its strength
review.why: 2:286 closes the surah with a prayer: do not load us with more than we can bear.
